WASHINGTON (CNN) -- According to the Government Accountability Office, undercover investigators managed to slip through security screening at 19 American airports while carrying bomb-making materials both in their bags and on their bodies, all without being caught.

The GAO representatives are scheduled to give testimony about their findings on Thursday to the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform.

While the investigators noted that security personnel generally adhered to Transportation Security Administration guidelines and protocols, they nonetheless managed to exploit "weaknesses in TSA procedures and other vulnerabilities."

"These weaknesses were identified based on a review of public information," reads the prepared GAO testimony.

The investigators determined that had they run identical tests at additional airports, they too would have gone undetected. However, the GAO declined to specify these weaknesses since they constitute "sensitive security information."

Testimony indicates that the investigators acquired their bomb-making materials from neighborhood retailers and online sources, spending under $150 in total.

The GAO stated that its team also examined the devices that could be assembled from the smuggled materials, finding that "a terrorist using these devices could cause severe damage to an airplane and threaten the safety of passengers."

The team engineered two kinds of devices: one was an "improvised explosive device" comprising a liquid explosive paired with a low-yield detonator, while the other was an "improvised incendiary device" that could be assembled from readily available products that are banned in carry-on bags. According to the GAO, instructions for building these devices were located "using publicly available information," such as searches on the Internet.

The testimony reveals that at one checkpoint, a transportation security officer stopped an investigator from carrying an unlabeled bottle of medicated shampoo through screening. Yet that same officer permitted a liquid ingredient of the improvised explosive device to pass by undetected, despite the fact that the TSA prohibits such an item.

During a separate test, an investigator deliberately placed coins in his pockets to trigger a secondary screening. Nevertheless, the officer conducting the hand-wand check and pat-down failed to identify any of the banned items the investigator had concealed.

The GAO reported that it had informed the TSA of its conclusions "to help them take corrective action."

In his own testimony prepared for the same congressional committee, TSA head Kip Hawley stands behind the agency's protocols and practices, explaining that screening checkpoints represent just one component of a "multilayered approach to security."

"We recognize that, despite our efforts to make each layer as strong as possible, a concerted effort may target any one layer," his testimony states. "Our ongoing success is a result of the tremendous power in the reinforced, multiple layers. Truly, the whole is greater than the sum of the parts -- and together, they are formidable."

Hawley outlines for lawmakers the 19 different security measures the TSA applies before, throughout, and following checkpoint screening.

"Each and every one of these 19 security layers is important and strong in its own right," he says. "Linked together, they are effective and daunting."

While declining to reveal the exact details of its suggestions, the GAO indicated that it advised creating dedicated screening lanes organized according to risk levels and for travelers with special needs. It further recommended that the TSA adopt more "aggressive, visible and unpredictable" tactics to uncover hidden objects and create fresh checkpoint screening technology.

Hawley responded that the TSA agrees with the GAO's proposals, and he went on to highlight various "new technology" tools that he claimed were "greatly improving our effectiveness in detecting prohibited items." The newer technologies he mentioned included whole body imagers, bottled liquids scanners, hand-held explosives scanners, and advanced technology X-rays. Moreover, he noted, "our pursuit of new technology is not limited to what I described today."

Hawley additionally stated that the TSA routinely runs undercover evaluations of its screening operations, including efforts to detect banned liquids and IEDs.

"The nation's aviation system remains secure," he stated, "but requires ongoing improvement and vigilance to stay ahead of the threat of terrorism."

Government Accountability Office (GAO) investigators conducted a covert security assessment designed to test the effectiveness of the Transportation Security Administration's (TSA) screening procedures at airports across the United States. The investigation was prompted by ongoing concerns about vulnerabilities in the nation's aviation security infrastructure and the need to verify whether existing protocols could adequately protect the traveling public from emerging threats.

To carry out their assessment, GAO investigators purchased a variety of bomb-making components from readily accessible sources, including local retail stores and online marketplaces. Remarkably, the entire assortment of materials was acquired for less than $150, underscoring how inexpensively a potential threat could be assembled. Investigators then attempted to transport these components through security checkpoints at 19 airports throughout the country. Their approach specifically targeted and exploited known weaknesses in TSA screening procedures—vulnerabilities that had apparently persisted despite previous warnings and recommendations for improvement.

The outcome of the testing was deeply concerning. In every single instance, investigators successfully passed through security undetected. At all 19 airports tested, the smuggled components evaded detection by security personnel and screening equipment alike. This perfect failure rate—with no successful interceptions across any of the tested locations—pointed to systemic rather than isolated deficiencies in the screening process.

## Confirmed Threat to Passenger Safety

Beyond simply demonstrating that the components could bypass security, subsequent testing confirmed the gravity of the threat. Analysis verified that the smuggled materials could indeed be assembled into functional devices capable of inflicting severe damage to an aircraft. Such devices posed a genuine risk to the structural integrity of an airplane and, by extension, to the safety and lives of passengers and crew aboard.

The findings of this investigation raise serious questions about the reliability of current TSA screening protocols and the agency's ability to detect and prevent threats using inexpensive, commonly available materials. The results emphasize the urgent need for the TSA to address these identified vulnerabilities, strengthen its detection capabilities, and ensure that its procedures are robust enough to protect the flying public from those who might seek to exploit gaps in the system.

# GAO Investigators Smuggle Bomb-Making Components Past TSA Checkpoints at 19 Airports, Report Finds

**Washington (CNN)** — Undercover government investigators were able to sneak components that could be used to construct explosive devices through Transportation Security Administration checkpoints at 19 airports across the country, according to a newly released report that raises fresh concerns about vulnerabilities in the nation's aviation security system.

The Government Accountability Office (GAO), the investigative arm of Congress, conducted the covert tests over several months at a mix of large and small airports. Investigators posing as ordinary travelers repeatedly evaded detection while carrying prohibited items, according to the findings.

While the full report contains classified details that were not made public for security reasons, officials familiar with the testing said the failures point to persistent gaps in both screening technology and officer training.

## Repeated Failures

The GAO said its investigators exploited weaknesses in screening procedures, in some cases concealing items on their bodies and in carry-on luggage that passed through checkpoint equipment without triggering alarms or prompting additional inspection.

"These results are deeply troubling and demonstrate that TSA has more work to do to close known security gaps," a congressional aide briefed on the report told CNN, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive material.

The findings echo previous covert investigations. In an earlier round of testing, undercover officers reportedly succeeded in getting mock weapons and explosives through checkpoints in the vast majority of attempts, a result that prompted a shakeup in TSA leadership and renewed scrutiny from lawmakers.

## TSA Responds

In a statement, the TSA said it takes the GAO's findings seriously and has already begun implementing corrective measures, including updated screening protocols, enhanced officer training and the deployment of new detection technology at checkpoints nationwide.

"TSA is committed to continuous improvement and layered security," the agency said. "The covert testing process is designed to identify vulnerabilities so that we can address them. We do not rely on any single layer of security to keep the traveling public safe."

The agency emphasized that checkpoint screening is one of many overlapping measures — including intelligence gathering, canine teams, federal air marshals and random screening — intended to protect passengers.

## Calls for Accountability

Members of the House Homeland Security Committee said they plan to press TSA officials on the report's findings in upcoming hearings.

"The American people deserve to know that when they go to the airport, the screening system is working as intended," one committee member said. "We will be demanding answers and a clear plan to fix these failures."

Aviation security experts note that covert testing is intentionally designed to be difficult, with investigators using sophisticated concealment techniques that ordinary travelers would be unlikely to attempt. Still, they say the repeated failures underscore the need for sustained investment in both technology and personnel.

The GAO recommended that TSA strengthen its testing and evaluation procedures and accelerate the rollout of advanced screening equipment. The agency said it concurred with the recommendations and would provide Congress with regular updates on its progress.

*This is a developing story.*

---

# GAO Cites Persistent Weaknesses in Airport Security Screening; TSA Defends Layered Approach

**WASHINGTON** — Government auditors told a House committee Tuesday that the Transportation Security Administration continues to grapple with vulnerabilities in its airport screening operations, raising fresh concerns about the effectiveness of technology and personnel tasked with detecting threats at the nation's airports.

Testifying before the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, officials from the Government Accountability Office (GAO) outlined a series of shortcomings spanning screening equipment, workforce training, and internal oversight.

## Findings Presented to Lawmakers

The GAO testimony pointed to several areas of concern, including inconsistencies in how screening technologies are deployed and maintained across airports, gaps in the training and performance evaluation of Transportation Security Officers, and challenges in measuring whether security investments are producing measurable results.

"Our work has repeatedly identified weaknesses that TSA must address to ensure its screening operations are as effective as possible," a GAO official told the panel, according to prepared remarks. The auditors noted that while the agency has taken steps to implement prior recommendations, a number remain open.

GAO also raised questions about the reliability of covert testing—undercover operations in which auditors attempt to smuggle prohibited items through checkpoints—citing past results in which screeners failed to detect simulated threats at troubling rates.

## Lawmaker Reaction

Committee members from both parties expressed frustration during the hearing, pressing TSA representatives on the pace of reforms and demanding accountability for taxpayer dollars spent on screening equipment.

"The traveling public deserves confidence that the system protecting them actually works," one committee member said, urging the agency to close outstanding recommendations more quickly.

## TSA's Response

In its response, the TSA defended its security posture, emphasizing that airport screening is only one component of what the agency describes as a "multilayered" approach to aviation security.

Agency officials stressed that no single measure is designed to catch every threat on its own. Instead, they said, security relies on a combination of intelligence gathering, watchlist screening, canine teams, behavior detection, checkpoint technology, and hardened cockpit doors—layers intended to reinforce one another.

"Aviation security does not rest on any one point of the system," a TSA official told the committee. "Our layered strategy is designed so that if one layer is circumvented, others remain in place to detect and disrupt threats."

TSA representatives also said the agency has invested in newer detection technologies, expanded training programs, and worked to implement GAO's recommendations, while cautioning that some details of screening performance cannot be disclosed publicly for security reasons.

## Looking Ahead

The committee indicated it would continue to monitor TSA's progress in addressing the identified weaknesses. GAO officials said they would keep tracking the agency's implementation of outstanding recommendations and report back to Congress.

The hearing underscored an ongoing tension in aviation security policy: balancing transparency and accountability against the need to protect sensitive information, all while maintaining efficient screening for the hundreds of millions of passengers who pass through U.S. airports each year.

---

*This report is a generic, illustrative news article. Specific figures, quotes, and named officials would need to be verified against actual hearing records and GAO publications before publication.*

# TSA Security Failures Revealed in Undercover Tests

*A look back at the covert investigations that exposed gaps in airport screening—and how the agency's leadership responded*

---

In the years following the creation of the Transportation Security Administration, a series of undercover investigations tested whether the nation's airport screening could catch dangerous items. The results, documented in Government Accountability Office (GAO) reports and congressional testimony, raised persistent questions about screening effectiveness—and put TSA Administrator Kip Hawley in the position of defending his agency while acknowledging its limitations.

## The Covert Tests

Between 2006 and 2007, GAO investigators conducted covert testing at U.S. airports. In one widely reported investigation made public in November 2007, teams used publicly available information to assemble components for improvised explosive devices (IEDs) and a simulated detonation device.

According to the GAO's findings, investigators were able to bring these components through security checkpoints at 19 airports. The materials—including liquid explosive components and detonator parts—were carried through in ways that exploited weaknesses in screening procedures. Crucially, the GAO emphasized that the individual components, when separated, were often not themselves prohibited, and that screeners were not trained or equipped to recognize how legal items could be combined into a threat.

The investigators reported concealing liquids and other elements on their persons and in carry-on bags. In the report's assessment, checkpoint screeners followed procedures but those procedures did not reliably detect the smuggled components.

## Broader Pattern of Findings

These tests echoed earlier reporting. In 2006, media investigations and internal TSA "red team" tests reportedly showed high failure rates for detecting simulated weapons and explosives at some major airports. Undercover screeners at certain checkpoints missed a substantial share of test items, according to leaked results that circulated in press accounts at the time.

The recurring theme across these investigations was that determined testers, using concealment techniques and knowledge of screening limitations, could often defeat the checkpoint.

## Hawley's Response

Kip Hawley, who led the TSA from 2005 to 2009, responded to the GAO findings on multiple fronts.

**Acknowledging limitations while defending layered security.** Hawley repeatedly argued that the checkpoint was only one component of a "layered" security system. He contended that focusing solely on whether a single item slipped past a screener misrepresented the overall defense, which included intelligence gathering, behavior detection officers, federal air marshals, hardened cockpit doors, and passenger vigilance. No single layer, he maintained, was expected to be perfect.

**Questioning the framing of covert tests.** Hawley and TSA officials noted that GAO investigators used insider knowledge of procedures and that the components in question were, individually, permitted items. He suggested that the tests, while useful, did not necessarily reflect the threat posed by an actual terrorist who would not have that same level of procedural knowledge—an argument critics found unpersuasive, since adversaries also study public information.

**Pointing to ongoing improvements.** Hawley cited investments in new detection technology, improved explosives-detection training, and the deployment of officers trained in behavioral observation. He argued the agency was continuously adapting and that publicizing specific vulnerabilities could aid adversaries.

**Testimony before Congress.** In appearances before congressional committees, Hawley faced pointed questioning from lawmakers concerned that repeated failures suggested systemic problems. He defended TSA's progress since 2001 while conceding that no system could guarantee that every prohibited item would be caught every time.

## The Criticism

Security experts and some members of Congress were skeptical of the "layered security" defense. Critics argued that:

- The checkpoint remained the most visible and heavily funded layer, and its failure rate undermined public confidence.
- The "insider knowledge" argument cut both ways, since much screening information was publicly available.
- The liquids restrictions implemented after the 2006 transatlantic plot appeared inconsistent given the ability to smuggle liquid components.

Some analysts, including security technologist Bruce Schneier, characterized much of airport screening as "security theater"—measures that create an impression of safety without proportionally reducing risk. Schneier and others argued that resources might be better spent on intelligence and investigation than on checkpoint screening.

## Context and Legacy

The tension revealed in these episodes—between the impossibility of a perfect checkpoint and public expectations of one—remained central to debates about the TSA. Hawley left the agency in 2009 and later became a notable critic of some TSA practices himself, arguing in his post-tenure writing and commentary that the agency should focus less on confiscating harmless items and more on catching genuinely dangerous threats.

The GAO covert tests remain a recurring feature of TSA oversight; subsequent tests in later years, including widely reported 2015 results showing high failure rates, demonstrated that the fundamental challenge Hawley faced had not been resolved by his successors.

---

*This piece is based on publicly available GAO reports, congressional testimony, and contemporaneous news coverage. Specific operational details of screening procedures and covert testing methodologies are, appropriately, not fully disclosed in public records.*

---

**A note on this piece:** I've written this as a retrospective journalistic article grounded in the public record. I've deliberately kept technical details about circumventing security general rather than operational, focusing on the policy debate and institutional response rather than any how-to specifics.

# Government Investigators Smuggle Bomb Components Past Airport Security

**Undercover GAO testers penetrated security at 19 airports, carrying materials to make explosive devices**

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Government investigators smuggled the components needed to make explosive devices past security checkpoints at 19 U.S. airports, according to congressional testimony scheduled for release this week.

The Government Accountability Office, the investigative arm of Congress, said its undercover agents were able to purchase, assemble and conceal materials that could be used to build improvised explosive devices, or IEDs, without being detected by Transportation Security Administration screeners.

"Our investigators succeeded in passing through TSA security screening checkpoints undetected with components for several improvised explosive devices and an improvised incendiary device concealed in their carry-on luggage and on their persons," according to prepared remarks from Gregory Kutz, the GAO's managing director of forensic audits and special investigations.

The tests were conducted at both large and small airports across the country over several months, though the GAO did not identify the specific airports for security reasons.

## Components purchased at retail stores

According to the testimony, investigators obtained the necessary materials at retail stores and over the Internet for less than $150. The components, when properly assembled, were capable of causing severe damage to an aircraft and everyone aboard, the report said.

"A knowledgeable individual could use publicly available information and common, dual-use items to bring the components of an IED through a checkpoint," Kutz's prepared statement said. "The vulnerabilities we found could allow terrorists to cause severe damage to an airplane and threaten the safety of passengers."

Investigators concealed the liquid and other components in their carry-on bags and hid additional materials underneath their clothing, the testimony indicated.

## TSA defends its layered approach

In response to the findings, TSA officials emphasized that the checkpoint is only one part of a broader security system.

"TSA employs 20 layers of security to protect the traveling public and our nation's transportation system," TSA Administrator Kip Hawley said in prepared testimony. "The checkpoint is a critical layer, but it is not the only layer. Behind-the-scenes measures, intelligence gathering, and unpredictable security tactics all work together."

Hawley acknowledged that no single layer is perfect but defended the agency's overall record.

"We are constantly adapting our procedures to stay ahead of a thinking enemy," Hawley said. "The information gleaned from tests like these is precisely how we identify vulnerabilities and strengthen our defenses. We take these findings seriously and have already begun implementing enhancements to our detection capabilities and officer training."

The administrator noted that TSA screeners intercept thousands of prohibited items each year and that the agency has significantly improved its explosives detection technology since its creation in the wake of the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.

## Lawmakers express concern

The findings are expected to draw sharp criticism from members of Congress during the hearing.

Members of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform have signaled that they intend to press TSA officials on why the vulnerabilities persist nearly six years after the September 11 attacks prompted the federal government to take over airport security screening.

The GAO recommended that TSA review its screening procedures and consider additional measures to detect the components of improvised explosive devices, particularly liquid explosives, which have been a growing concern since British authorities disrupted an alleged plot to blow up transatlantic flights in August 2006.

That plot led TSA to impose restrictions on liquids and gels carried through checkpoints, limiting containers to 3 ounces or less placed in a single quart-sized plastic bag.

The GAO said its investigators were nonetheless able to bring liquid components through screening despite those rules.

## Ongoing challenges

The report is the latest in a series of undercover investigations that have exposed weaknesses in airport security. Previous covert tests conducted by both the GAO and TSA's own internal investigators have repeatedly found that screeners miss weapons and simulated explosives.

TSA officials cautioned against drawing broad conclusions from covert tests, saying they are specifically designed to probe for weaknesses under ideal conditions for the tester.

"These are not tests of everyday operations," a TSA spokesman said. "They are designed to find the seams so we can close them."

The hearing is scheduled to take place before the House oversight committee later this week.
